experiment.title: Fidget spinner spin-down
experiment.headline: Rubbing friction c = 0.9000 ± 0.0014 rad/s²
experiment.blurb: Wonder guessed exponential decay. The held-out frames said otherwise.
experiment.description: Flicked a fidget spinner on a table and filmed it from above.

scene.description: A fidget spinner lying flat on a table, filmed from above, with a dot sticker on one arm. It is flicked once and spins down to rest. An A4 sheet lies flat beside it.

tracked_objects.why: Its angle around the hub gives the spin angle.

initial_hypotheses.name: Viscous friction
initial_hypotheses.mechanism: Friction proportional to speed, like a paddle in honey: the spinner loses the same fraction of its spin every second.
initial_hypotheses.observable_signature: ω(t) must fall by the same fraction each second, so log ω is a straight line. A constant-slope ω(t) that hits zero in finite time refutes it.

initial_hypotheses.name: Coulomb and viscous friction
initial_hypotheses.mechanism: Both at once: a constant rubbing term plus a term that grows with speed.
initial_hypotheses.observable_signature: ω(t) is slightly curved, steeper at first. If the fitted b is indistinguishable from zero, the viscous term is not needed.

initial_hypotheses.name: Coulomb friction
initial_hypotheses.mechanism: Rubbing friction in the bearing that does not depend on speed: the spinner loses the same amount of spin every second.
initial_hypotheses.observable_signature: ω(t) is a straight line and the spinner stops abruptly at t = ω₀/c. Curvature in ω(t), steeper at first, refutes it.

models.name: Viscous friction
models.mechanism: Friction proportional to speed, like a paddle in honey: the spinner loses the same fraction of its spin every second.
models.refuting_signature: ω(t) must fall by the same fraction each second, so log ω is a straight line. A constant-slope ω(t) that hits zero in finite time refutes it.
models.rejection_reason: Held-out RMSE 34.1 rad against 0.0234 rad for Coulomb and viscous friction: 1460× worse, and the intervals do not overlap (29.7 to 37.7 rad). An exponential never reaches zero, but the real spinner stopped at about 32.7 s: the model kept spinning through the whole last third of the clip.

models.name: Coulomb friction
models.mechanism: Rubbing friction in the bearing that does not depend on speed: the spinner loses the same amount of spin every second.
models.refuting_signature: ω(t) is a straight line and the spinner stops abruptly at t = ω₀/c. Curvature in ω(t), steeper at first, refutes it.
models.rejection_reason: Held-out RMSE 33 rad against 0.0234 rad for Coulomb and viscous friction: 1411× worse, and the intervals do not overlap (30.5 to 35.3 rad). A constant deceleration cannot bend: the real ω(t) is steeper at the start and shallower at the end.

models.name: Coulomb and viscous friction
models.mechanism: Both at once: a constant rubbing term plus a term that grows with speed.
models.refuting_signature: ω(t) is slightly curved, steeper at first. If the fitted b is indistinguishable from zero, the viscous term is not needed.

models.name: Coulomb friction and air drag
models.mechanism: Rubbing friction plus air drag that grows with the square of the speed.
models.refuting_signature: Drag dominates only at high spin and fades quickly, so ω(t) bends the other way: sharply at first, then almost straight.
models.rejection_reason: Held-out RMSE 9.77 rad against 0.0234 rad for Coulomb and viscous friction: 418× worse, and the intervals do not overlap (8.59 to 10.7 rad). Quadratic drag removes far too much spin early and then almost none.

quantities.name: Rubbing friction (per unit inertia)
quantities.note: Depends only on timing: angles need no scale.

confidence_reasons: S2 beat the runner-up on all three splits (50%, 65% and 80%).
No systematic pattern is left in its residuals.
No quality flags: tripod, level, sheet fully visible, no aliasing (largest step 41° per frame).
The reviewer challenged once, Wonder answered with numbers, and the reviewer then accepted.
caveats: The rubbing and viscous terms are per unit of inertia; a spinner's mass distribution cannot be seen on video, so absolute torques are not claimed.
A viscous term and a quadratic air-drag term cannot be separated by this clip alone; S3 is rejected on shape, not on mechanism.
conclusion.narrative_md: The spinner slows down by a **steady rubbing term** (0.9000 ± 0.0014 rad/s²) plus a **small speed-dependent term** (0.035001 ± 0.000029 1/s). My first guess, pure viscous friction, was **refuted**: it predicted a spinner that never stops, and this one stopped at 32.7 s. The prediction for the last third of the clip missed by 34 rad (RMSE), against 0.023 rad for the winner.

rounds.summary: The headline is plausible, but the second parameter is carrying more weight than the evidence shows. I want to see that b is needed.

issues.claim: S2 beats S1 because of the viscous term b.
issues.evidence: S1 held-out RMSE 33 rad, S2 0.023 rad. b = 0.035 1/s is small; the intervals depend on one 65% split.
issues.detail: Refit both models with the split at 50% and at 80%, and report whether b stays away from zero.

issues.evidence: The last 1.3 s of the clip are flat, but the angle estimate is only exact to ±0.015 rad.
issues.detail: Say that the stop time is read from where ω reaches zero in the fit, not observed directly.

rounds.response_md:
**Refit at 50% and 80%.** S2 wins both: held-out RMSE 0.017 rad at 50% and 0.016 rad at 80%, against 48 and 20 rad for S1. In all three fits b stays at 0.035 1/s with an interval that excludes zero.

**Caveat added:** the stop time is read from the fit's ω(t) reaching zero.

rounds.summary: The refits answer the objection: the viscous term is needed on every split and the advantage is far larger than the interval. Accepted.

events.title: Clip normalized
events.body_md: Read **2041 frames** at 60 fps (constant frame rate). Time factor 1, jitter 0.4%. Every frame has a real timestamp.

events.title: Wonder watched the clip
events.body_md: A fidget spinner lying flat on a table, filmed from above, with a dot sticker on one arm. It is flicked once and spins down to rest. An A4 sheet lies flat beside it.

tracked_objects.why: Its angle around the hub gives the spin angle.

events.title: SAM 3.1 tracked 2 objects
events.body_md:
- "blue dot sticker" (marker): Its angle around the hub gives the spin angle.
- "black spinner hub" (pivot): The center of rotation.

events.title: Scale and timing calibrated
events.body_md: The A4 sheet gives **0.52 mm per pixel** with 0.40% uncertainty. Plane offset 0 cm; camera moved 0.3 px over the clip.

events.title: Hypothesis S0: Viscous friction
events.body_md:
Friction proportional to speed, like a paddle in honey: the spinner loses the same fraction of its spin every second.

$$\dot\omega = -b\,\omega \;\Rightarrow\; \omega(t)=\omega_0\,e^{-bt}$$

**Refuted if:** ω(t) must fall by the same fraction each second, so log ω is a straight line. A constant-slope ω(t) that hits zero in finite time refutes it.

events.title: Hypothesis S2: Coulomb and viscous friction
events.body_md:
Both at once: a constant rubbing term plus a term that grows with speed.

$$\dot\omega = -c - b\,\omega$$

**Refuted if:** ω(t) is slightly curved, steeper at first. If the fitted b is indistinguishable from zero, the viscous term is not needed.

events.title: Hypothesis S1: Coulomb friction
events.body_md:
Rubbing friction in the bearing that does not depend on speed: the spinner loses the same amount of spin every second.

$$\dot\omega = -c \;\Rightarrow\; \omega(t)=\omega_0 - c\,t$$

**Refuted if:** ω(t) is a straight line and the spinner stops abruptly at t = ω₀/c. Curvature in ω(t), steeper at first, refutes it.

events.title: Hypothesis S3: Coulomb friction and air drag
events.body_md:
Rubbing friction plus air drag that grows with the square of the speed.

$$\dot\omega = -c - k\,\omega^{2}$$

**Refuted if:** Drag dominates only at high spin and fades quickly, so ω(t) bends the other way: sharply at first, then almost straight.

events.title: Prediction made before any fit: Viscous friction
events.body_md:
Before looking at a single fit, I expect **Viscous friction**. I will count it refuted if this happens: ω(t) must fall by the same fraction each second, so log ω is a straight line. A constant-slope ω(t) that hits zero in finite time refutes it.

The harness scores every model on the last 35% of the motion, which I never see.

events.title: Fit S0: Viscous friction
events.body_md:
Fitted on the first 65% of the motion, then forecast the rest.

- φ₀: **-4.875** (-5.98 to -3.77) rad
- ω₀: **58.26** (57.9 to 58.6) rad/s
- b (viscous friction): **0.06485** (0.0643 to 0.0654) 1/s

Training RMSE **1.96 rad**. Held-out RMSE **34.1 rad** (29.7 to 37.7). Lowest on 0 of 3 splits.

events.title: Fit S1: Coulomb friction
events.body_md:
Fitted on the first 65% of the motion, then forecast the rest.

- φ₀: **6.429** (5.31 to 7.55) rad
- ω₀: **51.37** (51.1 to 51.6) rad/s
- c (rubbing friction): **1.94** (1.92 to 1.96) rad/s²

Training RMSE **2.31 rad**. Held-out RMSE **33 rad** (30.5 to 35.3). Lowest on 0 of 3 splits.

events.title: Fit S2: Coulomb and viscous friction
events.body_md:
Fitted on the first 65% of the motion, then forecast the rest.

- φ₀: **-0.001593** (-0.0119 to 0.00868) rad
- ω₀: **55** (55 to 55) rad/s
- c (rubbing friction): **0.8995** (0.898 to 0.901) rad/s²
- b (viscous friction): **0.03502** (0.035 to 0.0351) 1/s

Training RMSE **0.0152 rad**. Held-out RMSE **0.0234 rad** (0.0212 to 0.0252). Lowest on 3 of 3 splits.

events.title: Fit S3: Coulomb friction and air drag
events.body_md:
Fitted on the first 65% of the motion, then forecast the rest.

- φ₀: **-0.6177** (-0.766 to -0.469) rad
- ω₀: **55.67** (55.6 to 55.7) rad/s
- c (rubbing friction): **1.402** (1.39 to 1.41) rad/s²
- k (air drag): **5.67e-4** (5.59e-4 to 5.75e-4) s/rad

Training RMSE **0.207 rad**. Held-out RMSE **9.77 rad** (8.59 to 10.7). Lowest on 0 of 3 splits.

events.title: Rejected S0: Viscous friction
events.body_md: Held-out RMSE 34.1 rad against 0.0234 rad for Coulomb and viscous friction: 1460× worse, and the intervals do not overlap (29.7 to 37.7 rad). An exponential never reaches zero, but the real spinner stopped at about 32.7 s: the model kept spinning through the whole last third of the clip.

events.title: Rejected S1: Coulomb friction
events.body_md: Held-out RMSE 33 rad against 0.0234 rad for Coulomb and viscous friction: 1411× worse, and the intervals do not overlap (30.5 to 35.3 rad). A constant deceleration cannot bend: the real ω(t) is steeper at the start and shallower at the end.

events.title: Rejected S3: Coulomb friction and air drag
events.body_md: Held-out RMSE 9.77 rad against 0.0234 rad for Coulomb and viscous friction: 418× worse, and the intervals do not overlap (8.59 to 10.7 rad). Quadratic drag removes far too much spin early and then almost none.

events.title: Winner: Coulomb and viscous friction
events.body_md: Coulomb and viscous friction predicts the held-out frames better than every rival, by more than the uncertainty.

events.body_md:
The headline is plausible, but the second parameter is carrying more weight than the evidence shows. I want to see that b is needed.
